story: H.R. 9340 would make a 100 megawatt customer pay the full cost of the grid built to serve it, and excuses any state whose legislature already voted on a comparable standard. Alaska's Senate voted on May 16th and its House never did.

claims.claim: The short title of H.R. 9340 is the Ratepayer Protection Act.
The reported version of H.R. 9340 carries House Report number 119-814.
claims.verbatim: [Report No. 119-814]

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 sits on the Union Calendar as number 713.
claims.verbatim: Union Calendar No. 713
claims.notes: Union Calendar placement means reported and eligible for floor action, which is not the same as scheduled. See C20 and C21.

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 was reported in the House on September 10th, 2026 in the second session of the 119th Congress.
claims.verbatim: 119th CONGRESS 2d Session

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 defines a large-load customer around a peak electric demand of 100 megawatts or more.
claims.verbatim: have, in the aggregate, a peak electric demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus
claims.notes: Aggregate PEAK DEMAND, which is power. Not nameplate generation and not annual energy.

claims.claim: The 100 megawatt threshold in H.R. 9340 is measured at a single site or campus.
claims.verbatim: at a single site or campus

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 reaches customers whose facilities require electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure for data storage and computational applications.
claims.verbatim: require electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure and related systems pertaining to data storage and computational applications and services
claims.notes: The bill never uses the phrase data center in its definition. It describes one functionally.

claims.claim: The large-load customer definition in H.R. 9340 applies only to a non-residential consumer requesting or entering a contract on or after the date of enactment.
claims.value: on or after the date of the enactment
claims.verbatim: means a non-residential electric consumer that, on or after the date of the enactment of this paragraph, requests to enter into, or enters into, a contract
claims.notes: Forward looking only. Existing contracts are untouched.

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 would require rates to a large-load customer to be designed to recover the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission or distribution upgrade needed to serve that customer.
claims.verbatim: shall be designed to recover from the large-load customer the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve the load of such large-load customer
claims.notes: The operative sentence of the bill.

claims.claim: The cost recovery requirement in H.R. 9340 continues to apply if the large-load customer terminates its contract or stops buying power.
claims.verbatim: including in the event of such large-load customer terminating a contract or other agreement with the electric utility pertaining to the sale of electric energy, or otherwise ceasing the purchase of electric energy
claims.notes: The stranded asset clause, and the strongest ratepayer-facing element in the bill.

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 gives each State regulatory authority one year after enactment to commence consideration of the standard or set a hearing date.
claims.verbatim: Not later than 1 year after the date of enactment of this paragraph, each State regulatory authority
claims.notes: The clock runs from enactment. No calendar date may be attached to it.

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 gives each State regulatory authority two years after enactment to complete consideration and make a determination.
claims.verbatim: Not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of this paragraph, each State regulatory authority
claims.notes: A state must consider and determine. It is not compelled to adopt.

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 excuses a state from the consideration requirement if the state acted before the date of enactment of the subsection.
claims.verbatim: shall not apply to the standard established by paragraph (22) of section 111(d) in the case of any electric utility in a State if, before the date of enactment of this subsection
claims.notes: The cutoff is a date of enactment that has not happened, so this is a closing window and never a missed deadline. Alaska's possible claim under the third prong is retrospective, since the May 16th Senate vote already sits before any future enactment date, so it does not depend on the Legislature reconvening.

claims.claim: The first way a state qualifies for the H.R. 9340 exemption is having already implemented the standard or a comparable standard.
claims.verbatim: the State has implemented for the electric utility the standard (or a comparable standard)

claims.claim: The second way a state qualifies for the H.R. 9340 exemption is having conducted a proceeding to consider implementing the standard.
claims.verbatim: has conducted a proceeding to consider implementation of the standard (or a comparable standard) for the electric utility
claims.notes: This is the prong a state utility commission can satisfy on its own, with no legislature.

claims.claim: The third way a state qualifies for the H.R. 9340 exemption is that the state legislature has voted on implementation of the standard.
claims.verbatim: the State legislature has voted on the implementation of the standard (or a comparable standard) for the electric utility
claims.notes: One chamber of the Alaska Legislature took a recorded vote on what may be a comparable standard (C38, C39). Whether a one chamber vote satisfies the State legislature has voted is unresolved, because the bill is not law and no state has had to argue it. This is the deck's central tension and it is posed as a question.

claims.claim: The House Committee on Energy and Commerce advanced the Ratepayer Protection Act by a vote of 52 to 0.
claims.verbatim: the Committee's passage of H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, by a vote of 52-0
claims.source_outlet: U.S. House Committee on Energy and Commerce

claims.claim: The Energy and Commerce committee vote on H.R. 9340 is reported by the committee under a July 21st, 2026 post.
claims.verbatim: by a vote of 52-0
claims.source_outlet: U.S. House Committee on Energy and Commerce
claims.notes: The date is the post date rather than a quoted sentence, so it is softened. The gap between a July committee vote and a September 10th report is the checkable thing.

claims.claim: Energy and Commerce Chairman Brett Guthrie said the Ratepayer Protection Act will ensure that data centers pay their own way instead of passing costs onto hardworking families.
claims.value: data centers pay their own way
claims.verbatim: The Ratepayer Protection Act will ensure that data centers pay their own way, instead of passing costs onto hardworking families.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. House Committee on Energy and Commerce

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 does not appear on the published House floor schedule at docs.house.gov as read on September 13th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: No.
claims.source_outlet: Office of the Clerk, U.S. House of Representatives
claims.notes: Verified negative, corroborated independently by C21. Write not yet scheduled, never scheduled or expected.

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 does not appear on the House majority leader's published schedule as read on September 13th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Neither H.R. 9340 nor the Ratepayer Protection Act is mentioned anywhere
claims.source_outlet: Office of the House Majority Leader

claims.claim: The White House says 23 governors signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.
claims.verbatim: 23 Governors signed on, representing the states where data-center growth is heaviest.
claims.notes: The page names no individual governor, so the deck may cite 23 and must not name who.

claims.claim: The White House says more than 300 organizations committed to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.
claims.verbatim: 300+ Organizations committed across every stakeholder in the U.S. power system.

claims.claim: The Ratepayer Protection Pledge asks signers to build, bring or buy every kilowatt their facilities need.
claims.verbatim: build, bring, or buy every kilowatt their facilities need
claims.notes: The executive branch and this House bill converge on the same principle by different instruments, one voluntary and one statutory.

claims.claim: The Department of Transportation request for information on America's Great Corridors of Commerce carries docket number DOT-OST-2026-3269.
claims.verbatim: [Docket No.: DOT-OST-2026-3269]
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, U.S. Department of Transportation

claims.claim: Comments on the Department of Transportation corridors request for information are due by October 2nd, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Written comments are due by October 2, 2026.
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, U.S. Department of Transportation

claims.claim: The Department of Transportation corridors notice says an aim is to incentivize data centers to locate close to the corridors for easy connectivity.
claims.verbatim: Incentivize data centers, manufacturing facilities, and distribution hubs to locate close to AGCC corridors to leverage a "plug and play" model for easy connectivity to new utility corridors
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, U.S. Department of Transportation
claims.notes: One arm of the federal government is recruiting data centers to the grid edge while another debates who pays for the upgrades they require.

claims.claim: The word Alaska does not appear in the Department of Transportation corridors request for information.
claims.verbatim: The word "Alaska" does not appear anywhere in this Federal Register document.
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, U.S. Department of Transportation
claims.notes: Verified negative, softened. Do not build a slide headline on the absence alone.

claims.claim: The Department of Energy request for information on securing the bulk-power system carries docket number DOE-HQ-2026-1123.
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, U.S. Department of Energy

claims.claim: Responses to the Department of Energy bulk-power system request for information are accepted on or before October 9th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Written responses, data, and information are requested and will be accepted on or before October 9, 2026.
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, U.S. Department of Energy

claims.claim: The Department of Energy notice says growth in advanced manufacturing, data centers, artificial intelligence and defense production has increased the nation's dependence on abundant, reliable electricity.
claims.verbatim: the rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, data centers, artificial intelligence, and defense production has increased the Nation's dependence on abundant, reliable electricity
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, U.S. Department of Energy
claims.notes: Quote the full list. Trimming it to data centers and AI alone overstates what DOE attributed to them.

claims.claim: The Department of Energy will hold a public webinar on the bulk-power system request for information on September 16th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: DOE will hold a public meeting via webinar on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, from 3 to 4 p.m. EDT.
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, U.S. Department of Energy
claims.notes: Three days after this run. 3 to 4 p.m. Eastern is 11 a.m. to noon in Anchorage.

claims.claim: The DeepGreen Cook Inlet preliminary permit application is docketed at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission as Project No. 15423-000.
claims.verbatim: Project No. 15423-000
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
claims.notes: Applicant of record is DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC.

claims.claim: Comments, motions to intervene and competing applications on the DeepGreen Cook Inlet permit are due by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 2nd, 2026.
claims.verbatim: by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 2, 2026
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
claims.notes: The only one of the three open rooms physically in Alaska.

claims.claim: The official title of Alaska Senate Bill 250 is An Act relating to data centers and relating to utility service for data centers.
claims.verbatim: An Act relating to data centers; and relating to utility service for data centers.
claims.notes: Secondary. akleg.gov refuses an automated read, so the primary title could not be seen. Attribute.

claims.claim: Alaska Senate Bill 250 was sponsored by Sen. Loki Tobin.
claims.verbatim: Löki Tobin (D)
claims.notes: Secondary, single source. The senator renders her name Loki with an umlaut.

claims.claim: Alaska Senate Bill 250 passed the Alaska Senate on May 16th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: was sent to the Alaska House of Representatives after passing the Senate on May 16, 2026
claims.source_outlet: Davis Wright Tremaine, Energy and Environmental Law Blog
claims.notes: The claim the deck turns on. Secondary, a named law firm energy practice, independently corroborated by C39. Attribute on the face of the slide.

claims.claim: BillTrack50 records Alaska Senate Bill 250 as having crossed over on May 16th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Crossed Over: 05/16/2026
claims.notes: Independent corroboration of C38. Crossed over means passing the originating chamber and moving to the other.

claims.claim: After Senate passage SB 250 was referred to the House Community and Regional Affairs Committee where it died.
claims.verbatim: Following Senate passage, SB 250 was referred to the House Community and Regional Affairs Committee, where it died.
claims.source_outlet: Davis Wright Tremaine, Energy and Environmental Law Blog

claims.claim: SB 250 would have required electric and gas utilities to enter commission-approved contracts with data center customers so that costs attributable to those facilities are borne by the operators rather than shifted to other customers.
claims.verbatim: requiring electric and gas utilities to enter into commission-approved contracts with data center customers and ensure that infrastructure and service costs attributable to those facilities are borne by the data center operators rather than being shifted to other customers
claims.source_outlet: Davis Wright Tremaine, Energy and Environmental Law Blog
claims.notes: A law firm's characterisation of the bill, not the bill's own words. Say according to Davis Wright Tremaine.

claims.claim: SB 250 included reliability safeguards meant to prevent data center demand from adversely affecting fuel supplies or utility service for existing customers.
claims.verbatim: The bill also includes reliability safeguards intended to prevent data center demand from adversely affecting fuel supplies or utility service for existing customers.
claims.source_outlet: Davis Wright Tremaine, Energy and Environmental Law Blog
claims.notes: A scope difference from H.R. 9340, which addresses cost recovery only and says nothing about fuel supply.

claims.claim: Committee amendments to SB 250 would have required data centers to provide financial security where serving them made a utility incur capital investment costs above 1 million dollars.
claims.verbatim: data centers must provide financial security when furnishing service to the data center will require an electric or gas utility to incur capital investment costs exceeding $1,000,000
claims.source_outlet: Davis Wright Tremaine, Energy and Environmental Law Blog
claims.notes: Alaska's trigger was a capital cost to the utility. The federal trigger is a customer's size. Different kinds of threshold, never two versions of one number.

claims.claim: The last recorded action on SB 250 was a House Community and Regional Affairs Committee hearing on May 18th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: House Community & Regional Affairs Hearing
claims.notes: A committee hearing, not a floor vote. The evidentiary basis for C46.

claims.claim: BillTrack50 lists SB 250 with a status of dead as of May 20th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Dead (as of 05/20/2026)
claims.notes: A tracker's status label, not a legislative act. It corroborates the adjournment date without sourcing the words sine die.

claims.claim: Neither available record shows the Alaska House ever taking a floor vote on SB 250.
claims.verbatim: where it died
claims.source_outlet: Davis Wright Tremaine, Energy and Environmental Law Blog
claims.notes: A negative proven by absence across two secondary records. Phrase as no House floor vote appears in the public record. Never write the House voted it down.

claims.claim: KTOO's Gavel Alaska archive lists SB 250 as data centers and utilities business in both a Senate floor session and the House Community and Regional Affairs Committee.
claims.verbatim: DATA CENTERS, UTILITIES
claims.notes: A weak third source, and the only primary one on this leg. It carries no dates and no tally. Its value is confirming the asymmetry, a Senate FLOOR session and only a House COMMITTEE.

killed.claim: Alaska has done none of the three things that would exempt it from the H.R. 9340 standard.
killed.why: Probably wrong on prong three, since the Alaska Senate voted on May 16th, and unknowable on prong two, since the Regulatory Commission of Alaska's docket record refuses an automated read. The story is the ambiguity, not a gap.

killed.claim: SB 250 died in committee without any floor vote.
killed.why: Overturned. It passed the Senate on May 16th before dying in a House committee. Any copy carrying the old framing is a factual error.

killed.claim: SB 250 passed the Alaska Senate by a specific vote tally.
killed.why: No yea and nay counts on any reachable page. The deck may say the Senate passed it and must not say by how much.

killed.claim: The Regulatory Commission of Alaska has, or has not, conducted a proceeding on large load or data center cost allocation.
killed.why: Nothing reachable in either direction. This is prong two and it is genuinely half the question. The deck must not claim it either way.

killed.claim: Gov. Mike Dunleavy signed the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge.
killed.why: The White House pledge page gives a count of 23 governors and names none of them. Dropped.

killed.claim: 187 organizations signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.
killed.why: Contradicted by the primary page, which says 300 plus. Using 187 would be a checkable error.

killed.claim: H.R. 9340 has a stated number of cosponsors.
killed.why: No cosponsor list was ever read. congress.gov refuses an automated read.

killed.claim: A member of the Alaska congressional delegation is or is not a cosponsor of H.R. 9340.
killed.why: No cosponsor list was read, in either direction. The deck says nothing about Begich, Sullivan or Murkowski and this bill.

killed.claim: H.R. 9340 is scheduled for House floor consideration.
killed.why: Affirmatively contradicted by two published schedules. It is on the Union Calendar, which means eligible, and on no schedule. The word scheduled must not appear near this bill.

killed.claim: The Regulatory Commission of Alaska faces a federal deadline on this question.
killed.why: Conditional on enactment, and the bill is not law. State it as would, if enacted.

killed.claim: The DeepGreen Cook Inlet project is a 100 megawatt load comparable to the H.R. 9340 threshold.
killed.why: The FERC notice calls its figure annual generation, which is energy, while the threshold is peak demand, which is power. Identical numerals, different quantities. Pairing them looks like the deck's best visual and would be its worst error.

killed.claim: The Alaska Legislature adjourned sine die on May 20th, 2026, and reconvenes January 19th, 2027.
killed.why: Neither the words sine die nor a reconvening date appear on any page reached this run. Use May 20th only in the form the sources support, that the bill was dead as of that date.

killed.claim: SB 250 is likely to be revived in a future legislative session.
killed.why: A law firm's forecast for its clients, not a fact. If used at all it is an attributed prediction.
